tips.title: Everything radiates, always
tips.body: **All bodies emit and absorb infrared at any temperature** — not just hot ones. Getting hotter does not start the radiating; it increases **how much per second** and shifts it to **shorter wavelengths**.

tips.title: A good absorber is a good emitter
tips.body: The same surface property works both ways. That is why **matt black** is used for solar panels, which must **absorb**, and for cooling fins, which must **emit**. Know one behaviour and you know the other.

tips.title: Constant temperature is a balance
tips.body: It does **not** mean the object has stopped radiating. It is **absorbing and emitting at the same rate**. Writing *it stops absorbing once it is warm* loses the mark, and it is the commonest error in this topic.

tips.title: Greenhouse gases add no energy
tips.body: They **slow the escape** of outgoing infrared, so the surface must get **warmer** before emission balances absorption. Saying they *add heat* or *trap the Sun's rays* misses what the balance argument is doing.

tips.title: Every factor changes one of two rates
tips.body: Reflection, cloud, ice, greenhouse gases — each acts by changing either the **rate absorbed** or the **rate emitted**. Say which one, and the rest of the answer follows without any extra facts.

tips.title: Same temperature, same distance
tips.body: For the Leslie cube, two controls decide whether the comparison means anything: every face at the **same temperature** (one cube, one lot of hot water, a lid) and the detector at the **same distance** from each. Then read the faces **quickly**, because the cube is cooling all the while. If the last face read is also the lowest, ask whether it was simply measured colder.

why.matters:
Everything warmer than absolute zero is glowing, in infrared, all the time: you, the walls, the ice in the freezer. The hotter it is, the more it gives off and the shorter the wavelengths, until at a few hundred degrees the glow creeps into visible red. This topic is that idea and its consequences.

The most important consequence is the balance: an object settles at the temperature where it absorbs as fast as it emits. That balance sets the temperature of a car in a car park, a desert at night, and the Earth.

examples.title: Why the black car is hotter in the car park
examples.body:
Two cars side by side in the sun, one white, one black, and the black one is too hot to touch. A matt black surface is the best absorber there is, close to the lesson's black body: it takes in nearly all the radiation landing on it. White reflects most of it away.

The balance then does the rest: the black car keeps absorbing faster than it emits until it is hot enough to emit as fast as it absorbs, and that is a higher temperature than the white car ever reaches. At night it reverses: black is also the best emitter, so the black car cools quickest.

boxes.title: White car, midday

boxes.title: Black car, midnight

boxes.title: White car, midnight

examples.title: Why a clear night means frost
examples.body:
A weather forecast that says *clear skies tonight* is warning of frost, and the reason is this topic's balance run at night. The ground radiates infrared upwards all the time. Under a clear sky that radiation goes straight out into space and nothing comes back, so the ground emits far faster than it absorbs and cools until the grass is below freezing.

Cloud changes the sum. A cloud absorbs the infrared coming up from the ground and radiates some of it back down, so the ground absorbs nearly as fast as it emits and stays mild. The difference between a frost and none is what is above the ground.

examples.title: What a thermal camera is looking at
examples.body:
A thermal camera shows a person as a bright shape on a dark street with no light at all. It is not seeing light. It is seeing **infrared**, which every object emits whatever its temperature, and it draws the picture from how much arrives.

The lesson's first fact is the whole instrument. Hotter objects emit more per second, so a face at body temperature glows more brightly on the screen than a wall, and a hot engine glows more than either. The camera is a map of what each surface is emitting at that moment. A mug of tea is a beacon, and footprints stay warm for a minute.

steps.title: Every object emits infrared
steps.body:
**All bodies — all objects — emit and absorb infrared radiation, no matter what temperature they are.** That includes you, this page, an ice cube and the walls of a cold room.

Two facts follow, and the specification asks for both.

**The hotter the body, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time.** Hotter does not mean it starts radiating; it means it radiates **more per second**.

**The intensity and the wavelength distribution of the emission both depend on the temperature.** A hotter object emits more radiation **and** shifts it towards **shorter** wavelengths. That is why a heating element glows dull red as it warms and orange-white when hotter still: at room temperature everything it emits is infrared, invisible to us, and only when it is hot enough does some of the emission reach visible wavelengths.

So objects do not divide into ones that radiate and ones that do not. **Everything radiates**; what changes with temperature is **how much** and **at which wavelengths**.

steps.title: What a perfect black body is
steps.body:
A **perfect black body** is defined precisely, and the definition is the mark:

**A perfect black body is an object that absorbs all of the radiation incident on it.**

And the consequence, which the spec states explicitly:

**A black body does not reflect or transmit any radiation.** If it reflected some, it would not be absorbing all of it; if it transmitted some, the same. Absorbing *all* of it leaves nothing for either.

Then the step that matters most:

**Since a good absorber is also a good emitter, a perfect black body would be the best possible emitter.**

That link between absorbing and emitting is not obvious and is regularly examined. A surface that is good at taking radiation in is equally good at giving it out — the two go together. So the best possible absorber is also the best possible emitter.

It explains why a **matt black** surface is used both for the panels of a solar heater, which must **absorb** as much as possible, and for the cooling fins of an engine, which must **emit** as much as possible. The same surface for opposite purposes, because it is good at both.

A note on the word: *black body* is about behaviour towards **all** radiation, not about visible colour. A perfect black body is a model — nothing is perfectly one — but many real surfaces come close.

steps.title: Required practical 10: the Leslie cube
steps.body:
Required practical 10 turns *a good absorber is a good emitter* into measurements. AQA's title for it covers both how much infrared a surface **emits** and how much it **absorbs**. The method in AQA's handbook measures emission, with a Leslie cube; absorption is usually shown with two plates beside a heater.

**Emission: the Leslie cube.** A hollow metal cube whose four upright faces are finished differently: **matt black**, **shiny black**, **matt white** and **shiny silver**. Fill it with **very hot water** from a kettle and put the lid on, so every face is at the **same temperature**. Point an **infrared detector** at each face in turn, the **same distance** from each, and record the reading.

**What you find.** The **matt black** face gives the highest reading and the **shiny silver** face by far the lowest, with the other two faces between them. Same temperature, so the difference is the **surface**: dull, dark surfaces are the best **emitters** of infrared, shiny light ones the worst.

**Absorption.** Two metal plates, one painted **matt black** and one **shiny silver**, are set the **same distance** from a **radiant heater**, with a thermometer against the back of each, or a drawing pin held on the back with a blob of **wax**. The **matt black** plate warms **faster** and its pin drops **first**: it is the better **absorber**. The same surface tops both lists, which is the point.

**Variables.** The **independent** variable is the surface. The **dependent** variable is the detector reading, or the temperature rise. **Control**: the **temperature** of the water, the **distance** from face to detector, and how long the detector is held there. The cube is **cooling all the time**, so take the four readings **quickly**, or in a different order on a repeat, so that no face is only ever measured after the water has cooled.

**Safety and sense.** The water is near boiling: fill the cube on a heatproof mat and do not move it. A liquid-in-glass thermometer with its bulb painted black works as a detector, but has the poorest **resolution**; an infrared thermometer or a thermopile is better.

steps.title: Higher tier: the balance that sets a temperature
steps.body:
This section is **Higher tier only**.

Every object is doing two things at once: **absorbing** radiation from its surroundings and **emitting** radiation of its own. Its temperature depends on which is happening faster.

**A body at constant temperature is absorbing radiation at the same rate as it is emitting radiation.**

And the change:

**The temperature of a body increases when it absorbs radiation faster than it emits radiation.**

The reverse is also true: emit faster than you absorb, and you cool. This is the whole of the Higher tier content, and it explains far more than it first appears.

steps.title: Higher tier: the temperature of the Earth
steps.body:
This section is **Higher tier only**, and it is where the black body idea earns its place on the specification.

The Earth's temperature is set by exactly the same balance, and the spec names the factors:

**The temperature of the Earth depends on the rates of absorption and emission of radiation, and on reflection of radiation into space.**

How it works:

1. Radiation arrives from the **Sun**, mostly at **short** wavelengths, including visible light.
2. Some is **reflected** straight back into space — by clouds, by ice, by light-coloured surfaces. That radiation never warms anything.
3. The rest is **absorbed** by the Earth's surface, which warms.
4. The warmed surface **emits** radiation of its own. Because the Earth is far cooler than the Sun, this emission is at **longer** wavelengths — **infrared**.
5. Some of that infrared escapes to space; some is **absorbed by gases in the atmosphere** and re-emitted, part of it back downwards.

The Earth's temperature settles where the rate of energy **arriving and being absorbed** equals the rate **leaving**. Change any of those and the balance point moves:

- **More reflection** — more ice, more cloud — means **less absorbed**, so a **lower** temperature.
- **More absorption in the atmosphere** — more greenhouse gases — means **less escapes**, so the surface must be **warmer** before the rates balance again.

The last point is the one to be able to state carefully. Greenhouse gases do not add energy; they **slow its escape**, so the Earth must reach a **higher temperature** before it emits fast enough to balance what it absorbs.

steps.title: Why the wavelengths matter
steps.body:
One detail explains why the atmosphere can trap heat at all, and it comes straight from the first step of this topic: **the wavelength emitted depends on the temperature**.

- The **Sun** is extremely hot, so the radiation reaching us is at **short** wavelengths — largely visible light, which passes easily through the atmosphere.
- The **Earth** is far cooler, so the radiation it emits is at **much longer** wavelengths — **infrared**.

The gases in the atmosphere are **not equally transparent to both**. They let the short-wavelength radiation through on the way in, but **absorb** a good deal of the long-wavelength infrared on the way out.

That asymmetry is the whole mechanism. Energy comes in easily and leaves with difficulty, so the surface must be warmer than it otherwise would be before the rates balance.

If the Earth emitted at the same wavelengths it received, the atmosphere would treat incoming and outgoing radiation alike and there would be no such effect. It is the **temperature difference between the Sun and the Earth** — and so the wavelength difference — that makes it work.

steps.title: Going deeper: constant does not mean nothing is happening
steps.body:
**The idea most answers get wrong.** When something is at a constant temperature, it is **not** because radiation has stopped. It is **absorbing and emitting at the same rate**. A radiator at a steady temperature is pouring out infrared every second and taking some in; a rock in the desert at midday is doing both furiously. Constant temperature is a **dynamic balance**, and saying so is what distinguishes a top answer.

The same error appears as *the object stops absorbing once it is warm*, or *at night the Earth stops emitting*. Neither is true. What changes is the **relative rates**.

**Why a good absorber is a good emitter.** The link is worth holding on to because questions build on it. A surface that readily takes radiation in is equally ready to give it out — it is the same interaction between radiation and the surface, run in opposite directions. So:

- **Solar panel**: wants to **absorb** as much as possible → **matt black**.
- **Cooling fins on an engine**: want to **emit** as much as possible → also **matt black**.
- **Survival blanket**: wants to **reduce emission** from the person → **shiny silver**, which is the worst emitter.
- **Radiator backing**: **shiny**, to reflect radiation back into the room.

If you know the surface, you know both behaviours; if you know one behaviour, you know the other.

**On the Earth, three precisions.**

- Greenhouse gases **do not add energy**. They **slow its escape**, so the surface must reach a **higher temperature** before it emits fast enough to balance.
- **Reflected** radiation is not absorbed at all, so it does no warming. More ice or cloud means more reflection and a lower temperature — which is why melting ice matters twice over: less ice reflects less, so more is absorbed, so more melts.
- The mechanism depends on **incoming and outgoing radiation having different wavelengths**, which is itself a consequence of the Sun and the Earth being at very different temperatures.

**And on the word *black*.** A perfect black body is defined by absorbing **all radiation**, including wavelengths we cannot see. It is a **model** — nothing is perfect — but matt black surfaces approximate it well, and the Sun itself is treated as one.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **All bodies emit and absorb infrared radiation**, whatever their temperature.
- The **hotter** the body, the **more** radiation it emits **in a given time**.
- The **intensity and wavelength distribution** of the emission both depend on the **temperature**; hotter means shorter wavelengths.
- A **perfect black body absorbs all of the radiation incident on it**.
- It therefore **reflects none and transmits none**.
- **A good absorber is also a good emitter**, so a perfect black body is the **best possible emitter**.
- **Matt black** absorbs and emits best; **shiny silver** does both worst.
- **Higher tier**: a body at **constant temperature** is absorbing **at the same rate** as it is emitting.
- Its temperature **rises** when it absorbs **faster** than it emits, and falls when it emits faster.
- Constant temperature is a **balance**, not an absence of radiation.
- **Higher tier**: the Earth's temperature depends on the **rates of absorption and emission** and on **reflection into space**.
- Radiation from the **Sun** is **short** wavelength and passes through the atmosphere; the **Earth** emits **long** wavelength infrared, much of which the atmosphere **absorbs**.
- Greenhouse gases **slow the escape** of energy rather than adding any, so the surface must be **warmer** to balance.
- **Required practical 10**: a Leslie cube of hot water, every face at the **same temperature**, the detector at the **same distance**; **matt black** emits most and **shiny silver** least, and the matt black plate by a heater warms **fastest**. Read the faces quickly, because the cube is cooling.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by a perfect black body, and explain why it would be the best possible emitter of radiation. Give two examples of surfaces chosen for how well they absorb or emit.
questions.solution: A perfect black body is an object that absorbs all of the radiation that is incident on it. Because it absorbs all of the radiation falling on it, there is none left to be reflected and none to be transmitted, so a perfect black body neither reflects nor transmits any radiation at all. A good absorber of radiation is also a good emitter of radiation, since the same interaction between the radiation and the surface works in both directions. It follows that an object which is the best possible absorber must also be the best possible emitter, which is why a perfect black body would be the best emitter there could be. In practice matt black surfaces come close to this behaviour, and they are chosen for that reason. The panels of a solar heater are painted matt black so that they absorb as much of the incoming radiation as possible, while the cooling fins on an engine are also painted matt black, but in their case so that they emit as much radiation as possible and lose heat quickly. A survival blanket, by contrast, is made shiny silver because a shiny surface is a poor emitter and so reduces the radiation lost by the person wrapped in it.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The definition.** A perfect black body **absorbs all of the radiation incident on it**.

**What follows.** With all the incident radiation absorbed, there is none left to **reflect** and none to **transmit** — so a black body does **neither**.

**Why it is the best emitter.** **A good absorber is also a good emitter**: it is the same interaction between radiation and the surface, working in both directions. So the **best possible absorber** must also be the **best possible emitter**.

**Examples.**

- A **solar heating panel** is **matt black**, to **absorb** as much radiation as possible.
- The **cooling fins on an engine** are also **matt black**, but to **emit** as much as possible.
- A **survival blanket** is **shiny silver**, a poor emitter, so the person loses less energy by radiation.

The first two are worth giving together: the same surface chosen for **opposite purposes**, which only makes sense once you know that absorbing and emitting go together.

questions.prompt: Explain how the balance between absorbed and emitted radiation determines the temperature of the Earth, referring to reflection and to the effect of gases in the atmosphere.
questions.solution: Radiation arrives at the Earth from the Sun. Some of this radiation is reflected straight back into space by clouds, by ice and by pale surfaces, and because it is never absorbed it does no warming at all. The rest is absorbed by the Earth's surface, which warms as a result. The warmed surface then emits radiation of its own, but because the Earth is very much cooler than the Sun this emitted radiation is at much longer wavelengths, in the infrared. Some of this infrared escapes into space, and some of it is absorbed by gases in the atmosphere and re-emitted, part of it downwards towards the surface. The temperature of the Earth settles at the value for which the rate at which radiation is absorbed is equal to the rate at which it is emitted into space. If the rate of absorption were greater the temperature would rise, and a hotter surface emits more each second, so the temperature would rise only until the two rates balanced again. An increase in greenhouse gases does not add any energy to the Earth. What it does is absorb more of the outgoing infrared and so slow the escape of energy, which means the surface must reach a higher temperature before it is emitting fast enough to balance what it absorbs. An increase in reflection, from more ice or more cloud, has the opposite effect, because radiation that is reflected is never absorbed and so the temperature settles lower.

**Radiation arriving.** From the Sun. Some is **reflected straight back into space** by clouds, ice and pale surfaces — and because it is **never absorbed**, it does no warming at all.

**Radiation absorbed.** The rest is **absorbed by the surface**, which **warms**.

**Radiation emitted.** The warmed surface emits radiation of its own. Because the Earth is far **cooler** than the Sun, this is at **much longer wavelengths** — **infrared**.

Some escapes to space; some is **absorbed by gases in the atmosphere** and re-emitted, part of it back downwards.

**Where the temperature settles.** At the value where the **rate of absorption equals the rate of emission**. If absorption were greater the temperature would rise — and a hotter surface emits **more each second**, so it would rise only until the rates balanced again.

**Greenhouse gases.** They **add no energy**. They absorb more of the **outgoing infrared**, **slowing its escape**, so the surface must reach a **higher temperature** before it emits fast enough to balance.

**More reflection** — more ice, more cloud — does the opposite: reflected radiation is never absorbed, so the balance is struck at a **lower** temperature.

The framing that earns the marks is *balance*: every factor in the question acts by changing one of the two rates.

questions.prompt: Which face of a Leslie cube gives the highest reading on an infrared detector?
questions.solution: **Matt black** is the best emitter, so at the same temperature it gives the highest reading; **shiny silver** gives the lowest.

markScheme.description: Matt black

questions.prompt: In required practical 10, what is the independent variable when using a Leslie cube?
questions.solution: The **surface** is what is deliberately changed from face to face. The reading is measured, and the temperature and distance are kept the same.

markScheme.description: The type of surface

questions.prompt: Two metal plates, one matt black and one shiny silver, are placed at equal distances from a radiant heater. A drawing pin is stuck to the back of each with wax. What happens?
questions.solution: The **matt black** surface **absorbs** more of the radiation, so that plate warms faster, its wax melts sooner and its pin falls **first**. The shiny plate reflects most of the radiation away.

markScheme.description: The matt black plate's pin falls first, because it absorbs more

options: The shiny silver plate's pin falls first, because it reflects more
Both pins fall at the same time, because the distances are equal
Neither pin falls, because the plates only emit radiation
The matt black plate's pin falls first, because it absorbs more

questions.prompt: Why is the Leslie cube filled with very hot water rather than warm water?
questions.solution: Everything emits infrared at any temperature, but a **hotter** body emits **more per second**, so the readings are larger and the **differences** between faces stand out above the noise of the detector.

markScheme.description: Hotter, so it emits more and the faces are easier to compare

options: Warm water would make the shiny faces emit more than the dull ones
Hotter, so it emits more and the faces are easier to compare
Only very hot objects emit infrared radiation

questions.prompt: A student measures the four faces in the order matt black, shiny black, matt white, shiny silver, taking two minutes over each, and finds shiny silver much lower than the rest. Why might this overstate the difference?
questions.solution: The water is **cooling** throughout, so a face measured last is measured at a **lower temperature** and emits less for that reason alone. Read the faces **quickly**, and repeat in a **different order**, so the order is not confused with the surface.

markScheme.description: The cube cools as it goes, so the last face is measured colder

options: The detector warms up during the readings, so its later readings are high
Matt black must always be measured last for a fair test
Two minutes is too short for the detector to settle
The cube cools as it goes, so the last face is measured colder

questions.prompt: A Leslie cube of hot water is read from 10 cm. The shiny silver face gives a reading of 4 units and the matt black face 40 units. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.solution: Same water, so the same temperature; same distance; so the readings compare **emission** and nothing else: $40 \div 4 = 10$ times as much. Absorption was not measured here, and the faces are not at different temperatures.

markScheme.description: Matt black emits about ten times as much at this temperature

options: Matt black emits about ten times as much at this temperature
Matt black is ten times hotter than shiny silver
Shiny silver reflects ten times as much radiation as matt black
Matt black absorbs ten times as much as shiny silver

questions.prompt: Describe how you would use a Leslie cube to compare how much infrared radiation different surfaces emit, and explain how the results support the statement that a good absorber is also a good emitter.
questions.solution:
Fill the **Leslie cube** with **very hot water** and put the **lid** on, so all four faces, matt black, shiny black, matt white and shiny silver, are at the **same temperature**. Point an **infrared detector** at each face in turn from the **same distance**, and record the reading. Because the cube is **cooling** all the time, take the readings **quickly**, and repeat them in a **different order** so that no face is always measured last.

The **matt black** face gives the **highest** reading and the **shiny silver** face the **lowest**, with the other two between. Same temperature and distance, so the surface alone decides how much is **emitted**.

The absorption half uses two plates, matt black and shiny silver, the same distance from a radiant heater: the **matt black** plate warms **fastest**, so it is the best **absorber** too. The same surface wins both tests, which is what *a good absorber is also a good emitter* predicts, and a **perfect black body**, absorbing everything, would be the best emitter of all.

The absorption test (plates by a heater) shows matt black also absorbs best
The same surface tops both, as a black body would: the best absorber is the best emitter

examTechnique.body:
Say that all bodies emit and absorb radiation before saying what changes with temperature.

Give the definition of a perfect black body in the specification's words: it absorbs all the radiation incident on it.

When explaining a surface choice, say whether the object needs to absorb or to emit, then name the surface.

For a constant temperature, say the rates of absorption and emission are equal. Never say the object has stopped radiating.

For the Earth, name all three factors: absorption, emission and reflection into space.

Say that greenhouse gases slow the escape of energy rather than adding any.

For required practical 10, name the **surface** as the variable you change, the **detector reading** as what you measure, and the **temperature** of the water and the **distance** to the detector as what you keep the same. Say the cube is **cooling** while you read it, and how you allow for that.
examinerErrors: Saying only hot objects emit infrared radiation.
Saying an object at constant temperature has stopped absorbing or emitting.
Saying a black body is simply an object that is black in colour.
Saying a good absorber is a poor emitter.
Saying greenhouse gases add energy to the Earth.
Forgetting reflection when listing what the Earth's temperature depends on.
Saying the atmosphere traps radiation without explaining the difference in wavelength.
Saying a shiny surface absorbs well because it is bright.
Reading the four faces slowly in a fixed order, so the last face is always measured colder.
Saying the shiny face is colder, when every face of the cube is at the same temperature.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer treats temperature as a **balance of two rates** and uses that single idea for an object in sunlight, a cooling cup of tea and the whole Earth. It never says radiation has stopped — it says which rate exceeds which. It knows that absorbing and emitting are the same property, so it can explain why matt black suits two opposite purposes. On the Earth it is precise that greenhouse gases **slow the escape** rather than adding energy, and it explains the wavelength asymmetry that makes the effect possible at all.
